 Key Points
 RAP and IBR payments are calculated from adjusted gross income (AGI), so every dollar you put into a traditional 401(k), HSA, dependent care FSA, or similar pre-tax account lowers your student loan payment as well as your tax bill.
 The biggest levers are a 401(k), 403(b), 457(b), TSP, HSA, and care FSA. 
 A single borrower earning $82,000 who puts 10% into a 401(k) and maxes an HSA cuts a RAP payment from $547 to $347 a month, nearly $2,400 a year, on top of roughly $3,100 in tax savings.
 Your student loan servicer doesn’t care what you earn. It cares what your tax return says you earn, and those are two different numbers. Payments under the Repayment Assistance Plan (RAP) and Income-Based Repayment are calculated from adjusted gross income, and AGI is what’s left after pre-tax retirement contributions, health savings account deposits, and a handful of other adjustments come off the top.
 Yes, you can use your paystub, but unless your income has dropped, that will result in a higher payment for the same income (because your paystub always uses gross income).
 If you can reduce your federal income tax reported income, you can also shrink the income figure the Department of Education uses to set your bill, which makes a 401(k) election or a dependent care FSA one of the few legal ways to lower your student loan payment without earning less. 
 Below are ten ways to save, the 2026 limit for each, what they do and don’t do, and a worked example showing how far they move a real payment.

 Why Your AGI Sets Your Student Loan Payment
 Both current income-driven plans run off AGI. RAP charges 1% to 10% of your total AGI, with the rate set by which $10,000 bracket your AGI lands in, then subtracts $50 a month per dependent, as covered in our breakdown of how RAP works . 
 IBR charges 10% of discretionary income (15% for borrowers whose loans date from before July 2014), and discretionary income is your AGI minus 150% of the federal poverty guideline for your family size, per our IBR explainer .
 AGI is line 11 of Form 1040. It’s your total income minus the “above-the-line” adjustments on Schedule 1, and it’s calculated before the standard deduction, itemized deductions, and tax credits. That ordering is what matters: anything that comes off before line 11 lowers your student loan payment, and anything that comes off after it doesn’t. 
 Our AGI explainer walks through the full list of adjustments.
 Pre-tax payroll deductions work the same way, one step earlier. Traditional 401(k) contributions, HSA and FSA elections, and pre-tax health premiums never appear in box 1 of your W-2, so they never reach your tax return as income at all. 
 A borrower with an $82,000 salary and $12,600 in pre-tax contributions reports $69,400 of wages, and that’s the figure that gets recertified with your servicer .
 Which Pre-Tax Moves Lower Your AGI In 2026?
 The table below covers all ten moves, the 2026 limit for each, whether the money also skips Social Security and Medicare tax, and who each one fits. The rest of the article takes them one at a time, starting with the workplace retirement plan most borrowers already have.
 Pre-Tax Moves That Lower Your AGI In 2026 
 Move 2026 Limit Lowers AGI Skips FICA Best For 
 Traditional 401(k), 403(b), TSP $24,500 (+$8,000 at 50+) Yes No Anyone with a workplace plan 
 Governmental 457(b) $24,500 (separate limit) Yes No Public employees, PSLF borrowers 
 Health Savings Account $4,400 self / $8,750 family Yes Via Payroll High-deductible plan enrollees 
 Dependent Care FSA $7,500 per household Yes Yes Parents paying for child care 
 Health Care FSA $3,400 Yes Yes Predictable medical costs 
 Pre-Tax Health Premiums No cap Yes Yes Most employees (automatic) 
 Traditional IRA $7,500 (+$1,100 at 50+) Income Limits No No workplace plan or under the phase-out 
 SEP IRA Or Solo 401(k) Up to $72,000 Yes No Self-employed and side hustlers 
 Commuter Benefits $340/month transit + $340/month parking Yes Yes Transit riders and paid parkers 
 Student Loan Interest Deduction $2,500 Income Limits No Borrowers under the phase-out 
 Source: IRS. The College Investor. 
 1. Traditional 401(k), 403(b), And TSP Contributions
 The biggest lever for most borrowers is a traditional workplace retirement plan. For 2026, the IRS raised the employee deferral limit to $24,500 for 401(k), 403(b), governmental 457(b), and Thrift Savings Plan participants, with an $8,000 catch-up at age 50 and an $11,250 catch-up for workers aged 60 to 63. Our 401(k) contribution limits page tracks the full history.
 Every pre-tax dollar you defer reduces box 1 wages one for one. Borrowers leaving an employer match on the table should start there, since the match is free money that also sits outside AGI.
 The “catch” is the Roth option. Roth 401(k) contributions are made with after-tax dollars and do nothing to your AGI, so a borrower who wants a lower payment needs the traditional bucket, even if a Roth would otherwise fit their long-term plan. 
 Our Roth 401(k) breakdown covers when that trade-off is worth it. The short version for forgiveness-track borrowers is that the traditional side wins.
 2. 457(b) Plans: A Second $24,500 For Public Employees
 If you work for a state or local government and have access to both a 403(b) or 401(k) and a 457(b), you can max both. The IRS treats the 457(b) limit as separate, so it isn’t combined with your 401(k) or 403(b) deferrals, which means a teacher, a nurse at a public hospital, or a city employee can shelter $49,000 of salary in 2026 before touching an HSA. 
 Our 403(b) vs. 401(k) comparison explains how the plans differ.
 That stacking matters most for borrowers pursuing Public Service Loan Forgiveness , who are exactly the people most likely to have a 457(b). 
 Every dollar of payment you avoid across 120 qualifying payments is a dollar forgiven tax-free at the end, so a public employee who can afford to fund both plans is lowering a bill that would otherwise be money gone.
 3. Health Savings Account (HSA)
 An HSA is the only account on this list that skips income tax, payroll tax, and your student loan payment at the same time. For 2026, the limit is $4,400 for self-only coverage and $8,750 for family coverage, plus a $1,000 catch-up at 55, and you need a high-deductible health plan with a deductible of at least $1,700 (self-only) or $3,400 (family) to qualify. 
 Our HSA explainer covers eligibility in detail.
 Contribute through payroll if you can. HSA contributions made through an employer’s cafeteria plan are excluded from Social Security and Medicare wages under IRS Publication 15-B , which a 401(k) deferral can’t match. Contributions you make directly are still deducted above the line on Schedule 1, so they lower AGI either way, but you’ll have already paid the 7.65% in FICA. 
 The best HSA providers let you invest the balance, which turns the account into a retirement fund with a student loan bonus attached.
 4. Dependent Care FSA
 Parents paying for daycare, preschool, after-school care, or summer day camp can run up to $7,500 a year through a dependent care FSA in 2026, up from $5,000, the first increase in 40 years. The money comes out before income and payroll taxes and never appears in AGI, and our dependent care FSA article runs the math: a married couple with a $105,000 AGI who contributes $7,500 drops from RAP’s 10% bracket to 9% and cuts their payment by about $144 a month.
 Two rules trip people up. The limit is per household, not per spouse, so a couple with two employers still caps out at $7,500 combined ($3,750 each if married filing separately). And any money you don’t spend by your plan’s deadline is forfeited, so elect what you know you’ll use. Once you recertify your income with the return that shows the contribution, the payment drop follows.
 5. Health Care FSA And Pre-Tax Insurance Premiums
 A health care FSA shelters up to $3,400 in 2026 for copays, prescriptions, glasses, and other medical costs, with a $680 carryover if your plan allows it. Like the dependent care FSA, the money skips income tax, FICA, and AGI. It’s a smaller lever, but a borrower with predictable medical spending gets the same triple benefit as an HSA without needing a high-deductible plan . If your employer offers both accounts, see how a health FSA compares with an HSA .
 Your health, dental, and vision premiums almost certainly already come out pre-tax through a Section 125 plan, which is why your box 1 wages are lower than your salary. There’s no action to take there, but it helps to know that a more expensive plan tier bought with pre-tax dollars lowers AGI too. That isn’t a reason to over-insure, and good tax software will show you where each dollar lands on the return.
 6. Traditional IRA Contributions
 A traditional IRA lets you deduct up to $7,500 in 2026 ($8,600 at 50 and up) above the line, but only if you clear the income test. If you’re covered by a workplace plan, the IRS phases out the deduction between $81,000 and $91,000 of modified AGI for single filers and $129,000 to $149,000 for married couples filing jointly. If neither spouse has a workplace plan, there’s no income limit at all. Our IRA contribution and income limits page has every bracket.
 That phase-out makes the traditional IRA a second-tier move for most borrowers with a 401(k). A single borrower earning $95,000 with a workplace plan gets no deduction, and a nondeductible contribution doesn’t touch AGI. Where it shines is for borrowers without a workplace plan, gig workers, and lower earners, who can deduct the full amount and still have until the April filing deadline to make a contribution that counts for the prior year. Skip the Roth IRA for this purpose, since it’s a great account that does nothing for your AGI.
 7. Self-Employed Retirement Plans
 Freelancers, side hustlers, and business owners have the highest ceiling of anyone. A SEP IRA or solo 401(k) allows total contributions up to $72,000 in 2026, per the IRS limit announcement we covered , with a solo 401(k) letting you defer $24,500 as the employee plus a profit-sharing contribution as the employer. Our self-employed retirement plans comparison explains which one fits.
 Self-employment comes with two more above-the-line adjustments that most borrowers forget: half of your self-employment tax and 100% of your health insurance premiums both reduce AGI on Schedule 1. A borrower with $20,000 in side income who sends $5,000 to a SEP IRA, deducts $1,413 for half of self-employment tax, and pays $4,800 in self-employed health premiums has knocked more than $11,000 off the AGI their servicer will see at the next recertification .
 8. Commuter Benefits
 If your employer offers a qualified transportation plan, you can set aside up to $340 a month for transit and another $340 a month for parking in 2026, pre-tax. That’s as much as $8,160 a year for a borrower who drives to a paid garage and then takes a train, all of it excluded from box 1 wages and from FICA, and all of it invisible to the RAP formula .
 The money is use-it-or-lose-it within the plan’s rules, so match the election to what you spend. For a borrower on RAP sitting a few thousand dollars above a bracket line, a commuter election can be the cheapest way to cross it, and the RAP calculator will show whether you’re close enough for it to matter.
 9. The Student Loan Interest Deduction
 This one is circular, but it counts. You can deduct up to $2,500 of student loan interest above the line, which lowers the AGI used to calculate next year’s income-driven payment. For 2026, Rev. Proc. 2025-32 phases the deduction out between $85,000 and $100,000 of MAGI for single filers and $175,000 to $205,000 for joint filers, and our student loan interest deduction breakdown explains why married borrowers who file separately can’t claim it at all.
 For a borrower under the phase-out on IBR, $2,500 of deductible interest trims the payment by $250 a year. Under RAP it depends on where the bracket line falls. The deduction is automatic as long as you have your Form 1098-E, and most tax software fills it in for you.
 10. Smaller Adjustments That Still Count
 A few other Schedule 1 items reduce AGI and get overlooked. Teachers can deduct up to $300 of classroom expenses, and alimony on pre-2019 agreements is still deductible. Investors who sell losing positions can net up to $3,000 of capital losses against ordinary income each year, which lowers AGI dollar for dollar. 
 None of these is large on its own, but a borrower within $1,000 of a RAP bracket can use one to cross it, and the full list sits in our AGI explainer .
 One more benefit never touches AGI in the first place. Employers can pay up to $5,250 a year toward your student loans tax-free under Section 127, a provision the One Big Beautiful Bill Act made permanent, and our employer student loan assistance article explains how to ask for it. 
 The money isn’t income to you, so it lowers your balance without raising your payment.
 What Doesn’t Lower Your AGI?
 Most of what people think of as tax breaks happen below the line and leave your student loan payment untouched. The standard deduction, itemized deductions, the child tax credit, and the earned income credit all reduce your tax bill after AGI is set. Roth 401(k) and Roth IRA contributions are after-tax, so they do nothing. And the new deductions for tips, overtime, car loan interest, and taxpayers over 65 are claimed on the new Schedule 1-A, which the National Association of Tax Professionals confirms sits below the line, so a server deducting $25,000 of tips still has the full amount in AGI for RAP purposes , and the same goes for the charitable deduction for non-itemizers that begins in 2026.
 A lower AGI has side effects, most of them good. Contributions that skip FICA (HSA, FSA, commuter benefits, pre-tax premiums) slightly reduce the wages credited toward your future Social Security benefit. Lowering AGI can also pull you back under the phase-outs for the student loan interest deduction or the Saver’s Credit, which is a bonus rather than a cost.
 How Much Can Pre-Tax Contributions Lower Your Payment?
 Take a single borrower with no dependents earning $82,000 in 2026. With no pre-tax contributions, RAP puts them in the 8% bracket for a payment of $547 a month. IBR, charges 10% of everything above $23,940, or $484 a month. 
 Our RAP vs. IBR comparison explains why the two plans diverge from there.
 How Pre-Tax Contributions Change A $82,000 Borrower’s Payment 
 Scenario Pre-Tax Contributions AGI RAP Payment IBR Payment 
 No Contributions $0 $82,000 $547/mo 8% bracket $484/mo 
 401(k) At 5% $4,100 $77,900 $454/mo 7% bracket $450/mo 
 401(k) At 5% + HSA Max $8,500 $73,500 $429/mo 7% bracket $413/mo 
 401(k) At 10% + HSA Max $12,600 $69,400 $347/mo 6% bracket $379/mo 
 401(k) At 15% + HSA Max $16,700 $65,300 $327/mo 6% bracket $345/mo 
 Single borrower, no dependents, 2026 limits and poverty guidelines. IBR at 10% of discretionary income. Source: Department of Education, IRS, HHS. The College Investor. 
 The pattern worth noticing is the RAP cliff: moving from $82,000 to $77,900 of AGI drops the borrower from the 8% bracket to the 7% bracket, and because the lower rate applies to every dollar, the payment falls $92 a month on a $4,100 contribution. The next $4,400 (the HSA) stays inside the 7% bracket and saves only $26 a month. Then the step to $69,400 crosses into 6% and saves another $82. IBR has no cliffs, since every $1,000 of AGI reduction saves exactly $100 a year, which is why the RAP calculator is worth running before you set your election.
 The tax savings stack on top. On $12,600 of contributions, a borrower in the 22% bracket avoids about $2,772 in federal income tax, plus $337 in FICA on the HSA portion, for roughly $3,100 in tax savings and nearly $2,400 in lower payments. That’s about $5,500 a year of benefit from money that is still theirs, which beats any extra payment strategy on the table.
 When A Lower Payment Is The Wrong Goal
 Lowering your payment only saves money if you’re on a forgiveness track. If you’re pursuing PSLF or long-term IDR forgiveness, every dollar you don’t pay is a dollar forgiven , and these moves are close to free money. 
 However, if your plan is to pay the loans off in full, a lower required payment stretches the timeline, and on IBR the interest keeps accruing while you pay less. Before you optimize, decide which box you’re in.
 The pre-tax moves still make sense for a repayment-track borrower, because the tax savings are real regardless. The difference is what you do with the lower bill: a borrower paying in full should keep sending the old payment amount, or more, and treat the pre-tax contributions as a way to fund retirement and pay down debt at the same time. 
 One caution for RAP borrowers: our breakdown of how RAP works notes that paying more than the billed amount can cost you that month’s interest subsidy and principal match, so run the numbers before you overpay.
 When Does The Lower Payment Show Up?
 Not right away. The Department of Education pulls your AGI from your most recent federal tax return, so contributions you make during 2026 lower the AGI on the return you file in early 2027, and your payment adjusts at your next income recertification after that. A borrower who raises their 401(k) election in November 2026 won’t see a full-year effect until the 2027 return is in use, which could be 2028.
 That lag is a reason to act now instead of waiting for open enrollment to force the decision. Elect the full amount for 2027 this fall, make a prior-year traditional IRA contribution before the April deadline if you qualify, and the lower AGI compounds from there.
 It’s also important to note that if you are leveraging any of these tax deductions, you need to use your tax return. If you use an alternative method like your pay stub, it will use your gross income, not your net income. If you just start this in open enrollment, you have to use your tax refunds to certify your payment.
 What About Married Borrowers?
 Married couples filing jointly are measured on combined AGI, so both spouses’ pre-tax contributions count, and both spouses’ incomes count too. A non-borrowing spouse who maxes a 401(k) lowers the borrower’s payment just as much as the borrower’s own contributions do. 
 Filing separately pulls the spouse’s income out of the calculation under both RAP and IBR, but it also costs the student loan interest deduction, halves the dependent care FSA cap, and shrinks the traditional IRA deduction phase-out to $10,000 if you’re covered by a workplace plan. 
 Our married filing separately math compares the two paths.
 Bonus: A Lower AGI Can Help On The FAFSA Too
 Parents with college-bound kids get a second payoff. Under the FAFSA Simplification Act, the form no longer asks about pre-tax contributions to workplace retirement plans, which used to be added back as untaxed income. 
 The Student Aid Index now runs off the AGI on your tax return, so a parent who defers $24,500 into a 401(k) lowers both their RAP payment and the income figure colleges use when deciding how much a family can pay for college .
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Do 401(k) Contributions Lower My Student Loan Payment?
 Yes, if they’re traditional pre-tax contributions. They reduce the wages in box 1 of your W-2 and therefore your AGI, which is the figure RAP and IBR use to set your payment. Roth 401(k) contributions are after-tax and don’t change your AGI or your payment.
 Does An HSA Lower My Income-Driven Repayment Payment?
 Yes. HSA contributions reduce AGI whether you make them through payroll or on your own, up to $4,400 for self-only coverage or $8,750 for family coverage in 2026. Payroll contributions also skip Social Security and Medicare tax, which makes the HSA the most tax-efficient account on this list.
 Can I Use A Dependent Care FSA To Lower My RAP Payment?
 Yes. Up to $7,500 a year in 2026 comes out of your paycheck before taxes and never appears in your AGI. Our dependent care FSA article shows a family dropping a full RAP bracket with one election.
 Does The Standard Deduction Lower My AGI?
 No. The standard deduction, itemized deductions, and tax credits are applied after AGI is calculated, so they lower your tax bill but not your student loan payment. Only above-the-line adjustments and pre-tax payroll deductions change the number on line 11 of your return .
 How Soon Will My Payment Go Down After I Increase My 401(k)?
 After your next recertification using a tax return that reflects the contributions. Money deferred in 2026 shows up on the return you file in 2027, and your servicer applies it at the following annual recertification .
 Is It Worth Lowering My Payment If I’m Not Going For Forgiveness?
 The tax savings are worth it either way. The lower payment only saves you money on a forgiveness track, so a borrower paying in full should keep paying the old amount and use the pre-tax contributions to build retirement savings alongside the payoff plan .
